title: unexpected behaviour evaluating pool connections with tbl and mirai
description:
Hi there

First of all thank you for the work done in this package and secondly I'm not sure if this issue is more appropriate here or in `dbplyr`, so please feel free to move if required.

I am having issues evaluating pool connections using `tbl` when working in an asynchronous manner using `mirai`. Please find a reproducible example below. This are based on the mirai [vignette](https://mirai.r-lib.org/articles/databases.html) for handling databases.

Synchronous (working)
```
library(pool)
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

file <- tempfile()
con <- dbPool(drv = RSQLite::SQLite(), dbname = file)
dbWriteTable(con, "iris", iris)

# Works as expected by returning `tbl_Pool` object.
tbl(con, "iris")
```

Asynchronous (not working)
```
library(mirai)

file <- tempfile()

daemons(2)
everywhere({
  library(pool)
  library(dplyr)
  library(dbplyr)
  con <<- dbPool(drv = RSQLite::SQLite(), dbname = file)
}, file = file)

m <- mirai(dbWriteTable(con, "iris", iris))
m[] # Returns TRUE

m <- mrai(tbl(con, "iris"))
# Returns error
# Failed to collect lazy table
# Caused by error:
# bad_weak_ptr
m[]
```

I think this may have to do with how `db_collect.Pool` (again not sure if this is more appropriate in the dbplyr or pool repo) uses its current environment but I'm not sure.

Package versions:

R 4.5.0

dbplyr_2.5.0
dplyr_1.1.4
pool_1.04
mirai_2.5.1

Let me know if you need any more information.

description:

   pool::poolWithTransaction(con, function(conn) {

title: FR: retry configuration and onError callback
description:
Background: I'd like to create a shiny app which is able to reconnect to a database once the connection is lost (without crashing the active shiny session).

Currently, when using `dbPool` and the database server is shutdown (I stopped the PostgreSQL service for testing) after successfully establishing a connection, {pool} will retry 2 times and throw an error after a few seconds (default `validationInterval = 60`):

> <pool> Failed to activate and/or validate existing object.
> <pool> Trying again with a new object.
> Error: connection to server at "localhost" (::1), port 5432 failed: Connection refused (0x0000274D/10061)
> 	Is the server running on that host and accepting TCP/IP connections?
> connection to server at "localhost" (127.0.0.1), port 5432 failed: Connection refused (0x0000274D/10061)
> 	Is the server running on that host and accepting TCP/IP connections?
> Error: invoke_wrapped: throwing std::runtime_error

Unfortunately, (afaik) I don't have the possibility to configure this behaviour, e.g. retry 5 times wait x seconds or retry forever.

Furthermore, as this is happening in a background process I can't use `tryCatch` to write my own error handling for this case (also afaik) - maybe a `onError` callback could be added?

I would be pleased to hear your opinion on this - cheers

title: Intended use of database pools
description:
While reading the documentation at [https://rstudio.github.io/pool/articles/advanced-pool.html](https://rstudio.github.io/pool/articles/advanced-pool.html), I noticed that it might give the impression that increasing the number of connections in a database pool could help manage "spikes in traffic" (presumably in shiny or plumber applications).

However, since database pools and their underlying connections cannot be shared across process boundaries (e.g., via promise_futures), I am curious about how the intended use-case for database pools was envisioned, aside from the auto-connect feature. As far as I know, database operations (read/write) will always block. One could argue that different connections to the same database could, in theory, be checked out one after another. However, this seems to be an extremely esoteric usage pattern.

I think this information could benetif other (potential) users as well. Thx.

title: Support for DBI Method `dbFetch()`
description:
Most of my production jobs deploy to Kubernetes, where we aim to execute everything with minimal resources. This constraint necessitates batch processing in small increments. Previously, I utilized `DBI::dbFetch()` within my pipelines to handle data collection in batches and structured it as follows (pseudo-code):

`batch_data <- DBI::dbFetch(res, n = batch_size)`

For reference, here are the docs for `dbFetch()`: [dbi.r-dbi.org/reference/dbFetch.html](https://dbi.r-dbi.org/reference/dbFetch.html)

As the docs state, `res` represents an object inheriting from [DBIResult](https://dbi.r-dbi.org/reference/DBIResult-class.html) created by `DBI::dbSendQuery()`. I know `DBI::dbSendQuery()` won't work with {pool} but I've been able to replace most `DBI::dbSendQuery()` calls in my code with `pool::dbExecute()`.

Each time `dbFetch()` was executed within a loop, it'd intelligently fetch the next batch of records. There might be a more efficient method that I haven't yet discovered, but the alternative approach I currently employ with pool (_which is effective but gross_) involves manually setting `start_row` and `end_row` for each loop iteration and then executing a query like this:

```{r}
batch_data <- pool::dbGetQuery(
  conn,
  glue::glue(
    "WITH CTE AS (
       SELECT {input_tbl}.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY 1) AS row_num
       FROM {db}.{input_tbl}
    )
    SELECT CTE.*
    FROM CTE
    WHERE row_num >= {start_row} AND row_num <= {end_row}"
  )
)
```

A {pool}-compatible `dbFetch()` would be incredibly useful. If there's a simpler solution that I've overlooked, I would appreciate any guidance. This package has already been a lifesaver and is now an integral part of my team's production cron jobs. Awesome package! 🙏

- Returning and checking out the connection any time after the first.

title: Address Connection Drop In Manual
description:
Hello,
I am writing millions of rows to a `MySQL` database using a `Rcpp` iterator. At the end of each iteration, the application appends the rows resulted from that iteration to a database table on the server. The server is on a cloud.
There could be thousands of rows/iteration. The process is lengthy making connection drop likely.
Eventually, the connection drop is detected at the end of iteration when the writing to database is ready to start. 
When the connection is found dead, from the error messages I see that `dbPool` swaps objects in the pool trying to reconnect (or so I think, as the documentation lacks clarity and specifics at times).

Therefore I hope you could help me with these questions:

-  what are the "checked out" objects and why would they be needed? Could there be any examples showing their advantage over just using `conn = dbPool(...)`? 
-  does the argument `validationInterval` apply to objects in pool or to current connection or, only to checked out objects?
-  is the pool diminished by the `idleTimeout` and why?
-  is `dbPool` set to reconnect automatically if the connection is found dead by switching to the next object in the pool?
- are all connection objects in the pool dead when the connection drop originates at the server end? And if so,
-  would it help inserting a `dbIsValid` check followed by a custom function to reconnect in case 
`dbIsValid` is found **FALSE**?
- in case of successful reconnection will the writing continue from where it was interrupted (the iteration result resides in memory during this time) or will it start all over?
I could be wrong but I have found no mention on how connection drop is treated in `pool`'s Manual. 
Please try to address and/or clarify the procedures for these situations.
Thank you!

title: poolWithTransaction and fork/multicore
description:
I know that many DB driver packages warn against sharing one connection across multiple processes, but I'm also trying to find a pattern to allow for some multicore parallelism for some DB operations. My initial thought was that provided no connection was _simultaneously_ used across distinct processes, this might work. My initial script looked like the below and indeed, it works fine: ```R CONN_COUNT <- 2 CORE_COUNT <- 2 QUERY_COUNT <- 10 dbiconnpool <- pool::dbPool(RPostgres::Postgres(), service = "my.psql.service", maxSize = CONN_COUNT) # un-comment the following line to generate downstream SSL errors: #initial_query <- DBI::dbGetQuery(dbiconnpool, "select 1") foo <- parallel::mclapply(seq_len(QUERY_COUNT), function(i) { pool::poolWithTransaction(dbiconnpool, function(conn) { DBI::dbGetQuery(conn, "select 1") }) }, mc.cores = CORE_COUNT) foo ## either a collection of SSL errors or a collection of 1x1 dataframes with value 1. ``` However, if the `initial_query <- ...` line is un-commented out -- i.e. an upstream block where the `dbiconnpool` object fetches (and returns to the pool) a connection for a query -- **only now** the downstream querying fails do to various SSL errors reminiscent of https://github.com/jeroen/curl/issues/131. I'm a bit stumped as to why this example works when `initial_query <- ...` is skipped. My first guess was that the SSL connections are PID-dependent and I was getting 'lucky' with the multicore approach where each forked process was always fetching the same connection from {pool}, but the errors occur even when `initial_query <- ...` line is present and `CONN_COUNT <- 1` ... in such a case the `mclapply` call bypasses any actual forking, and so the PID is constant. I haven't yet tried to replicate this on a non Mac OS X system (where my SSL library is the system's LibreSSL (v2.8.3)). Has anyone else used {pool} in such a fashion to manage distinct database connections with multicore parallelism? I can ultimately do this myself by pre-chunking my data into `CONN_COUNT` groups while also keeping `CORE_COUNT < CONN_COUNT` and having each parallel-executing group manage opening and closing its own DB connection (i.e. similar in spirit to `poolWithTransaction()`). But before going down that path I figured I'd ask for thoughts here, as the `initial_query` oddity above is still quite confusing to me.

title: Best practices using pool with promises/future
description:
In the documentation for the `promises` package, [it states](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/promises/vignettes/futures.html):

> Future code blocks cannot use resources such as database connections and network sockets that were created in the parent process. This is true regardless of what future implementation you use! Even if it seems to work with a simple test, you are asking for crashes or worse by sharing these kinds of resources across processes.
> 
> Instead, make sure you create, use, and destroy such resources entirely within the scope of the future code block.

This means they are recommending to write future code blocks like:

```r
future({
  conn <- DBI::dbConnect(RMySQL::MySQL(), ...)
  result <- tbl(conn, "flights") %>%
    group_by(dest) %>%
    summarise(delay = mean(dep_time)) %>%
    collect()
  DBI::dbDisconnect(conn)
  result
})
```

I'd like to retain the `pool` package to manage database connections in my Shiny app, if possible.

**If I set a minimum pool size of zero and an idle timeout of zero, does this ensure that a new database connection is instantiated for each future code block?** (Thereby satisfying the requirements of the `promises` package.)

For example:

```r
pool <- pool::dbPool(
  RMySQL::MySQL(),
  minSize = 0,
  maxSize = 5,
  idleTimeout = 0,
  ...
)
future({
  tbl(pool, "flights") %>%
    group_by(dest) %>%
    summarise(delay = mean(dep_time)) %>%
    collect()
})
pool::poolClose(pool)
```

title: Automatically reconnect after de-serialization
description:
In one of my packages I have an object which internally stores a `tbl` / `tbl_dbi`. For parallelization, I now need to serialize this object to the file system so that a computational node can read the object, query the database and start its computation.

Unfortunately, as an external pointer, the connection becomes invalid during serialization / deserialization. My workaround for this is to reestablish the connection as illustrated in this code snippet:

```r
requireNamespace("DBI")
requireNamespace("RSQLite")
requireNamespace("dplyr")
requireNamespace("dbplyr")
requireNamespace("pool")

# create a tbl on iris stored in a SQLite db 
dbname = tempfile("db_", fileext = ".sqlite")
con = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), dbname)
# con = pool::dbPool(drv = RSQLite::SQLite(), dbname = dbname)
dplyr::copy_to(con, iris, "iris", temporary = FALSE)
data = dplyr::tbl(con, "iris")

# destroy the connection
tmp = tempfile()
saveRDS(data, file = tmp)
data = readRDS(tmp)

# verify it is disconnected
head(data) # -> error / invalid pointer
data$src$con
DBI::dbIsValid(data$src$con)

# reconnect
data$src$con = DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), dbname)

head(data)
```

As far as I understand it, `pool` as a connection manager should automatically reconnect, but I just get the same error if I replace the connection with a pool object ("external pointer is not valid").

title: Leaked pool objects during development
description:
I've created a single-file app using a pooled connection to a PostgreSQL server, per the instructions on [https://shiny.rstudio.com/articles/pool-basics.html](https://shiny.rstudio.com/articles/pool-basics.html).  When running the app in RStudio, we get many "leaked pool object" notifications when we:
1) run app
2) edit app.R, save, Reload app (repeat several times as developing)

```
> runApp('[path redacted]')

Listening on [localhost IP redacted]
Warning in (function (e)  : You have a leaked pooled object.
Warning in (function (e)  : You have a leaked pooled object.
Warning in (function (e)  : You have a leaked pooled object.
Warning in (function (e)  : You have a leaked pooled object.
```

The pool connection is stored in a local R package function:

```
get_pool() = function() {
     require(pool)
      con = dbPool(RPostgreSQL::PostgreSQL(), [redacted])
     return(con)
}
```

In the app.R code we just call the function to get our pool, e.g., `pool <- get_pool()` in place of storing the connection credentials in the app.R file.

It seems that these localhost pools just get leaked over and over again and never get cleaned up on our PostgreSQL server.  Eventually we surpass the 16-connection limit and have to manually kill the leaked connections.  This doesn't seem to happen when we're running the app on its normal server and accessing through a browser.

title: Embed pool in `dplyr::tbl`, not the raw connection
description:
When I create a dplyr::tbl() the database connection is baked into the resulting object. If my database connection is lost (the db restarted, I opened too many connections and the original connection got pruned, etc), then I can no longer get un-evaluated dplyr SQL back out of the tbl_dbi. Enter package:pool. Surely this will come to my rescue; surely the connection inside the tbl will be evaluated in a lazy fashion and fetched from the pool at runtime. But no such luck, a bare con is baked into the tbl.
```
library(RSQLite)
library(DBI)
library(dplyr)
library(pool)
dbPool(
  RSQLite::SQLite(), 
  dbname = ":memory:",
  validateQuery = "select 10"
) %>% 
  tbl(sql("select 1")) %>% 
  str()
```
If I'm using package:pool incorrectly and there is a right way to do this, please let me know. If I've an unreasonable expectation of what pool should do here, please let me know. I'd originally created an issue on dplyr (https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/3184), but Hadley recommended I open an issue on this passage instead.

title: Race condition in scheduler causes test failures
description:
After much investigation and the help of some R-Core members, it turns out that the seemingly-
random errors we've had on R-devel were caused by a race condition in the pool package.

Specifically, the NaiveScheduler's [`executeTasks`](https://github.com/rstudio/pool/blob/54bd256/R/scheduler.R#L72-L83) method could get invoked by a this [finalizer](
https://github.com/rstudio/pool/blob/54bd256/R/pool.R#L208-L218) when running the same `executeTasks` method. The error can be triggered reliably by inserting a `gc()` in the middle of `executeTasks()`.

If a `gc()` is inserted right after line 74, I reliably get this output, on R 3.3.3 and R-devel:

```
> source("testthat.R")
1. Error: fetch: only validates after validationInterval (@test-fetch.R#35) ----
could not find function "task"
1: naiveScheduler$protect({
       obj <- poolCheckout(pool)
       t0 <- Sys.time()
       pool_metadata <- attr(obj, "pool_metadata", exact = TRUE)
       lastValidated_t0 <- pool_metadata$lastValidated
       poolReturn(obj)
       obj <- poolCheckout(pool)
       t1 <- Sys.time()
       pool_metadata <- attr(obj, "pool_metadata", exact = TRUE)
       lastValidated_t1 <- pool_metadata$lastValidated
       if ((t1 - t0) * 1000 < pool$validationInterval) {
           expect_identical(lastValidated_t0, lastValidated_t1)
       }
       checkCounts(pool, free = 0, taken = 1)
       poolReturn(obj)
       checkCounts(pool, free = 1, taken = 0)
       obj <- poolCheckout(pool)
       t2 <- Sys.time()
       pool_metadata <- attr(obj, "pool_metadata", exact = TRUE)
       lastValidated_t2 <- pool_metadata$lastValidated
       if ((t2 - t0) * 1000 < pool$validationInterval) {
           expect_identical(lastValidated_t0, lastValidated_t2)
       }
       checkCounts(pool, free = 0, taken = 1)
       poolReturn(obj)
       checkCounts(pool, free = 1, taken = 0)
       Sys.sleep((pool$validationInterval + 100)/1000)
       obj <- poolCheckout(pool)
       t3 <- Sys.time()
       pool_metadata <- attr(obj, "pool_metadata", exact = TRUE)
       lastValidated_t3 <- pool_metadata$lastValidated
       if ((t3 - t0) * 1000 > pool$validationInterval) {
           expect_false(identical(lastValidated_t0, lastValidated_t3))
       }
       checkCounts(pool, free = 0, taken = 1)
       poolReturn(obj)
       checkCounts(pool, free = 1, taken = 0)
       obj <- poolCheckout(pool)
       t4 <- Sys.time()
       pool_metadata <- attr(obj, "pool_metadata", exact = TRUE)
       lastValidated_t4 <- pool_metadata$lastValidated
       if ((t4 - t3) * 1000 < pool$validationInterval) {
           expect_identical(lastValidated_t3, lastValidated_t4)
       }
       checkCounts(pool, free = 0, taken = 1)
       poolReturn(obj)
       checkCounts(pool, free = 1, taken = 0)
   }) at testthat/test-fetch.R:35
2: private$refCount$release() at testthat/test-fetch.R:35
3: private$callback()
4: self$protect({
       task()
   })
5: force(expr)

2. Error: pool scheduler: schedules things in the right order (@test-scheduling.R#13) 
could not find function "task"
1: naiveScheduler$protect({
       scheduleTask(1000, function() {
           results <<- c(results, 3L)
       })
       scheduleTask(100, function() {
           results <<- c(results, 2L)
       })
       scheduleTask(10, function() {
           results <<- c(results, 1L)
       })
   }) at testthat/test-scheduling.R:13
2: private$refCount$release() at testthat/test-scheduling.R:13
3: private$callback()
4: self$protect({
       task()
   })
5: force(expr)

testthat results ================================================================
OK: 204 SKIPPED: 0 FAILED: 2
1. Error: fetch: only validates after validationInterval (@test-fetch.R#35) 
2. Error: pool scheduler: schedules things in the right order (@test-scheduling.R#13) 
```

The problem is that there's a window of time between when the counter used by `protect` is [decremented](https://github.com/rstudio/pool/blob/54bd25636930f3823fe51feb755f41e643049fa1/R/scheduler.R#L112) and when it enters another `protect` block. If the finalizer fires in that window (as we did explicitly with the `gc()` above), then bad things can happen.

title: Make compatible with dbplyr
description:
1.  The implementation of the dplyr database backends has moved to dbplyr. Most of the generics remain in dplyr, so that existing backends don't break.

2. By inspecting the namespace, you can now easily see what methods you need to override for non-DBIConnections. Here's the complete list

````
 db_analyze
 db_begin
 db_collect
 db_commit
 db_compute
 db_copy_to
 db_create_index
 db_create_indexes
 db_create_table
 db_data_type
 db_desc
 db_drop_table
 db_explain
 db_has_table
 db_insert_into
 db_list_tables
 db_query_fields
 db_query_rows
 db_rollback
 db_save_query
 db_sql_render
 db_write_table
 sql_escape_ident
 sql_escape_string
 sql_join
 sql_select
 sql_semi_join
 sql_subquery
 sql_translate_env
 ````

3.  There are a lot of methods, but most of them simply require you to acquire the connection, then release it when it's done. To make that easier, I've written you this function to generate the wrapper functions:

``` r
 library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
 library(rlang)

pool_wrap <- function(f) {
 f <- enquo(f)

formals <- formals(eval_tidy(f))
 con <- names(formals)[[1]]
 passed_on <- names(formals[-1]) %>%
 set_names() %>% 
 lapply(as_symbol)

body <- expr({
 db_con <- poolCheckout(!!sym(con))
 on.exit(poolReturn(db_con))

UQE(f)(db_con, !!!passed_on)
 })

new_function(formals, body, f_env(f))
 }

pool_wrap(db_analyze)
 #> function (con, table, ...) 
 #> {
 #>     db_con <- poolCheckout(con)
 #>     on.exit(poolReturn(db_con))
 #>     db_analyze(db_con, table = table, ... = ...)
 #> }
 #> <environment: 0x7ff69c8927c8>
 ```

4.  There are at least two exceptions: `copy_to()` and `compute()` will need need to throw an error if `temporary = TRUE` because temporary tables are local to a connection, and there's no guarantee you'll get the same connection back next time.

I'm reasonably certain I've made all the changes to dbplyr to facilitate your Pool, but please let me know if I've missed anything. I'm also happy to hop on a call with you and @jcheng5 to answer any questions that you might have.

title: Hadley thinks the classes are wrong
description:
From my chat with @hadley (obviously feel free to edit if my transcription missed something...):

1. [this](https://github.com/rstudio/pool/blob/master/R/DBI-pool.R#L16-L18) doesn't seem right to me: you generally shouldn't be defining methods when you own neither the generic nor the class

2. [this](https://github.com/rstudio/pool/blob/master/R/DBI-pool.R#L42-L45) doesn't seem right either: an arbitrary DBI connection won't necessary have DBI metadata?

    You need `setOldClass("Pool")` and then you should bind to Pool rather than DBIConnection like you do in the rest of the package. Or if those are supposed to be specifically for connections returned by the pool, you probably need some wrapper class, like PooledConnection.

3. You should make `dbPool` inherit from DBIConnection. You've implemented all the DBI methods, so you've implicitly made it a DBI connection, and you should you acknowledge to the world that you implement the DBI connection interface.

    **Aside - some thoughts on OO:**
    > You should think of DBIConnection more of an interface than a subclass. So, by "inheriting" from DBIConnection, you're clearly stating that you fulfill the contract of the DBIConnection interface, which you do. (Technically calling it an interface is bit confusing because that makes you thinking of message-passing OO; calling it a concept is more in alignment with terminology of generic function OO.)

     Among other things, this would make implementation of `src_dbi` a lot easier, So we could have something like:

    ```r
    pool <- dbPool(
      drv = RMySQL::MySQL(),
      dbname = "shinydemo",
      host = "shiny-demo.csa7qlmguqrf.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com",
      username = "guest",
      password = "guest"
    )
    src <- src_dbi(pool)
    ```

title: Support for RSQLServer
description:
As far as I understand, the **RSQLServer** package creates a SQL backend to **dplyr** for connections to a MS SQL Server. The package creates the function `src_sqlserver` which is not one of the three standard types within the **dplyr** package. When I run the command `src_pool(pool) %>% tbl("TableName") %>% head(5)` as in the example using a pool connection created with the `RSQLServer::SQLServer()` driver it returned the following error:

> Error in UseMethod("tbl") : 
>   no applicable method for 'tbl' applied to an object of class "c('src_', 'src_sql', 'src')"

Upon examination of the `src_pool` function in the package code, I notice that the `pool$state$drv` is being set based on one of the three possible drivers that are supported by **dplyr**.  Thus, I created a separate function based on `src_pool` that replaces the `drv` variable with the string `"sqlserver"`.

It seems that an additional if statement in the `dbPool` function (above the `src_pool` function) that assigns the `pool$state$drv` value would fix this error easily - of course the latest **RSQLServer** package would need to be installed.

This package was the only way that I could find to connect to MS SQL Server and have a dplyr backend. Would it be possible to add the appropriate conditional statements to the `dbPool` function to support the `src_sqlserver` command from the **RSQLServer** package?

Example code, slightly modified `src_pool` function, and it returns the correct results:

```
src_pool_sqlserver <- function(pool2) {
    if (!requireNamespace("dplyr", quietly = TRUE)) {
      stop("dplyr package required", call. = FALSE)
    }
    gc()
    drv <- "sqlserver"
    conn2 <- poolCheckout(pool2)
    info <- dbGetInfo(conn2)
  dplyr::src_sql(drv, conn2, info = info, disco = NULL)
}

src_pool_sqlserver(pool) %>% tbl("TableName") %>% head(5)
```

Note, the pool connection was created as follows:

```
pool<-dbPool(drv=RSQLServer::SQLServer(),
             server="NAME_IN_sql.yaml"
  )
```

title: Stored procedures cause error
description:
If you use a query that relies on a stored procedure, your NEXT query using a connection from the same pool will fail unless you forcibly close the connection. 

```
 Error in mysqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) : 
  RS-DBI driver: (could not run statement: Commands out of sync; you can't run this command now) 
```

Example: 

```
pool <- dbPool(...)
con <- poolCheckout(pool)
ids <- c(1,2,3,4,5)
query <- paste0("CALL `sp`("ids,")", collapse = "")
rs <- dbSendQuery(con, query)
df <- dbFetch(rs, n = -1)
dbHasCompleted(rs) # TRUE
dbClearResult(rs) # TRUE
poolReturn(con)
```

After using the sp, your next query will fail with the error above.

I've tried a bunch of different things to try to see what's going on. But `dbHasCompleted` returns TRUE which is what you would hope after a fetch. Similariy, dbMoreResults() returns TRUE. So perhaps there's something we can do there.

title: Question about database example
description:
This is not an issue, just a question. Since currently R is single threaded, and the database operations are synchronous (AFAIK), the use of multiple connections to the database is quite limited in my opinion. But maybe I am missing something. Can you give an example where you actually benefit from pooling multiple connections? 

Keeping a single connection open is relatively easy, in a package I usually use sg like this:

``` r
internal_data <- new.env()
dbfile <- tempfile()
db <- function() {

  ## Check if connection is still valid, open a new one if not
  if (!exists("conn", envir = internal_data) || is.null(internal_data$conn) || dbIsValid(internal_data$conn)) {
    conn <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbfile)
    assign("conn", conn, envir = internal_data)
  }
  internal_data$conn
}
```

and then you can make queries with `dbSensQuery(db(), ...)`. You can also put the connection in a closure, if you are not writing a package.

Obviously, the `pool` package is still very useful for other use cases, but I just don't see why you would want multiple connections.

title: Should leaked connections be passivated (with a reap task set up) or actually destroyed?
description:
I feel like the first one makes a whole lot more sense (currently, we have the second one).

Again, consider the app from #3 :

``` r
library(shiny)
library(pool)
library(dplyr)

pool <- dbPool(drv = RSQLite::SQLite(), 
               "CollegeScorecard.sqlite")

ui <- fluidPage(
  actionButton("recalc1", "Re-query the database (1st table)"),
  tableOutput("tbl1"),
  actionButton("recalc2", "Re-query the database (2nd table)"),
  tableOutput("tbl2")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$tbl1 <- renderTable({
    n <- input$recalc1
    tbl <- src_pool(pool) %>% tbl("data") %>% 
      head(n + 3) %>% 
      select(year, id, school.name, school.state)
    info <- dbGetInfo(pool)
    print(paste("free:", info$numberFreeObjects,
                "taken:", info$numberTakenObjects))
    tbl
  })
  output$tbl2 <- renderTable({
    n <- input$recalc2
    tbl <- src_pool(pool) %>% tbl("data") %>% 
      head(n + 3) %>% 
      select(school.name, student.size)
    info <- dbGetInfo(pool)
    print(paste("free:", info$numberFreeObjects,
                "taken:", info$numberTakenObjects))
    tbl
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

Aside from the issue in #3 (let's assume here that was fixed), we're still not getting any performance benefits, because the leaked connections are automatically destroyed upon detection, rather than recycled (i.e. passivated and be ready for activation, at least until the reap task kicks in, depending on the `idleTimeout` param).

I'm pretty sure this change should be uncontroversial...

title: Long idleTimeout values stand in the way of effective garbage collection
description:
Suppose you have an app like:

``` r
library(shiny)
library(pool)
library(dplyr)

pool <- dbPool(drv = RSQLite::SQLite(), 
               "CollegeScorecard.sqlite")

ui <- fluidPage(
  actionButton("recalc1", "Re-query the database (1st table)"),
  tableOutput("tbl1"),
  actionButton("recalc2", "Re-query the database (2nd table)"),
  tableOutput("tbl2")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$tbl1 <- renderTable({
    n <- input$recalc1
    tbl <- src_pool(pool) %>% tbl("data") %>% 
      head(n + 3) %>% 
      select(year, id, school.name, school.state)
    info <- dbGetInfo(pool)
    print(paste("free:", info$numberFreeObjects,
                "taken:", info$numberTakenObjects))
    tbl
  })
  output$tbl2 <- renderTable({
    n <- input$recalc2
    tbl <- src_pool(pool) %>% tbl("data") %>% 
      head(n + 3) %>% 
      select(school.name, student.size)
    info <- dbGetInfo(pool)
    print(paste("free:", info$numberFreeObjects,
                "taken:", info$numberTakenObjects))
    tbl
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

In theory, since we're losing the reference to each connection as soon as the reactive is calculated, the connections should leak and be recycled immediately. However, that doesn't happen until after one min (which is the default `idleTimeout`). If you change this to 100 millis or something like that, you get the behavior you'd expect:

``` r
pool <- dbPool(drv = RSQLite::SQLite(), 
               "CollegeScorecard.sqlite",
               idleTimeout = 100)
```

Here's my current theory/educated guess: the `idleTimeout` is setting an attribute (for a reap task) on the connection. So we're _not_ actually losing the reference to the connection when we think we are, only after the reap job is and the attribute is lost...

This is obviously not what we want.
